speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This conversation with Frances Vaughn Fry took place at our home in Kendrick on August 3rd, 1976. The interviewer was Sam Schrager.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: There was two boys older than I was. After we lived here about a year I imagine it was or so, we moved up to Cedar Creek.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What year would this have been?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: About 18… that would have been... I was just three years old, it would have been 80 years ago. Oh, that would have been 1899 then probably.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It was 80 years ago that that happened?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, no. You're 80 years old. I'm 83 years old now. And I was three years old when we went to Cedar Creek. And my life has been right around this area ever since. Well then that would have been I think 1899. And we went up there, we was up there for... I lived up there until my family was practically grown. Then we moved down here again, we farmed up there. And then when my children were old, my youngest one was about... one year she was about... well I'd say 12, 14 years old. And I cooked in camps. Then I took... I helped with all farming on my dad's ranch until I was married. And then after I was married, my husband had a place up there and we lived there on his mother's place, that fry place. We lived there for 23 years. And then we moved to Kendrick. Our older children had graduated from Kendrick High School. The older children. And then I moved down here. I had the three youngest ones still was home with me when we moved down here. And then I went out to work. Well I did nursing, I went with the doctor. I was doctor's helper for many years. And then I worked for anyone that needed help. I had done housework, I'd done anything that they needed. Just worked and went places, you know, to stay maybe two or three weeks or something like that at a time. Well I kept that up for a good many years. And then I got this work that I worked for Mr. Israel, Clem Israel. I worked for him for oh, I guess 10 or 12 years. And cooking in a logging camp. And I had anywhere, she had a family and I had a family and she helped me too. And I worked in this logging camp for 10 or 12 years or something like that. And I took my three children with me, I had them with me all the time. And this three youngest ones. And then I went from there. I came, we were down here. That was when after we came down here. Then I still did nursing and went around different places. I'd help this one out at harvest time and that one out. And I cooked it for thrashers and anything that was to be had. But I had worked for Mr. Israel an earlier day at the ... And then he went to logging and I was all up around Clarkia and all up in that country for several years.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Boy, it sounds like you've really had a full life of work.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I have… i did that… and then after the children were all grown and gone. I worked for the forest service for 12 years. Well, I worked in all the stores around here in Kendrick before that. After we were down here and I worked anywhere they needed somebody. And I worked for pretty near all the store men at that time. The hardware and the grocery stores and just all the little stores around here. I worked for most of them. And I did that for many years. And then I got a chance to go from there. I was working for Marvin Long over here. And I worked for him for, well, I worked for Bluets first up here, Dick Bluets. And then I worked for Marvin Long. And finally the forest man, forestry man, they needed a cook at the forestry department. Taking these boys of two kids, you know, the eight, 16, 17, 18 year old boys. And I went with them as a crew. Well, I went to every place. I went up on Moscow Mountain. I was over to Osaka. I was up to Clarkia.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: To the work camps.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I didn't know. I was in sawmill or logging work at Clarkia. But the forestry work, I went up to the mountains up here first. And then I went from, just changed from place to place. I was over to Potlatch and I was up to, over to Osaka, wherever they needed. And at the time I went to work there. Why then we had to, if there was a fire, a big fire come. Why, I was supposed to go with my crew and cook at these fires and everything that was on. But I never did have to go on a big fire. They had a big outfit that is an outfit that would take care of a big lot of men. Because they had boilers and big kettles and all that stuff, you know, to take care of the crew. And then I worked for them for 12 years. And then when they quit, why, they didn't have then any more cooks on there. But boys would go back and forth. But I cooked for, had those boys and then I cooked for them. And then I cooked for the road man that was working on the road. Anybody that happened to be around with extra, I had a trailer house and all that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And... Well, let me go back and let's start at the beginning a little bit. Let me ask you a little about these really early days when you were just a youngster. And why was it that your family decided to move up on Cedar Ridge?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, they came from the east up here. My folks, my dad, they wanted a place. And they did think of buying up here right up on the hill here. And then they decided they got a chance to go up there. And they went up there when I was, I was four years old in March. When they moved up there. On Cedar Ridge. On Cedar Creek, yeah, Cedar Creek.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, were there, did they take a homestead on the...

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, they bought a place up there. It now is the Lions place. They, it's changed hands again now. It is the Lions place where we used to live.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did your father keep depot work or did he give it up and go to farming?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, my mother and the boys did the work. My mother and the oldest boy. And then there was a man that lived close there by us by the name of John Carr. And he helped my mother. And my dad still worked on the railroad. But he'd come home every so often, you know. Oh, sometimes it was sooner and sometimes... Because he went from, well, he was at St. Mary's and St. Joe and oh, just a lot of those places. And he went around and then of course he'd come home every once in a while. And she had this, this man helped her. But she and the boys did the work at home mostly. They, of course this man helped put in the crops and things. But my mother took care of the gardens and all of that stuff. She did all that herself with the boys' help.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now, your father, what was the work that he was doing on the railroad at that time?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: He was a railroad agent. Yeah, railroad agent.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That meant he had to travel around.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yes, wherever they called he'd get bumped maybe one place and then they'd put him off someplace else. And then he'd have to move again. That is when they were on the railroad. Then when they come this far then, they were at Crow Agency and back in Nebraska and all around different places like that. And then they kept coming out this way and then they finally come to Kendrick. But he wasn't the depot agent here at Kendrick. But he was depot agent around at the other places, St. Mary's and all places like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that it was kind of rough on your mother having to do a lot there by herself without, you know, generally you get the idea that the man took care of the farm.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, he didn't because he had this other man was a very good neighbor. He was a lovely man. He was a bachelor. And he helped him and my dad work together. You see there wasn't money in the country then and my dad would get the money. He was paid so much and he got money and this man would help my dad. Well, it would go from year to year when the year was up. Why they would go together and make out what he had done and what he had helped with and all like that. Well, my dad would pay him the money that he figured that he needed for the things that he had done. But my mother then just stayed on the farm and she well we raised our course. We had our garden and our cows and our pigs and all of that stuff like that you on any farm. But she took care of all that herself. She never she never had anyone but just the boys. The oldest boy was old enough to help her. And then she cleared. I can remember going out with my mother clearing timber, you know, off the ground, burning stumps and all of that stuff and piling up and chunking up the fires and all that stuff. I can remember that very funny.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How many children did she have at the time?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Just the three till later. She had two boys later, but they well one of them still alive. My youngest brother. I have just one brother left is all I had the four brothers.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did the kids like did you start helping her at an early age when you were still young?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Not particularly, no… i didn't have to do very much. I wasn't of course I wasn't old enough to do very much even to the good. But I didn't help her very much. But the first. Oh, I worked out a little bit before I was married, but then not very long.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, do you think that that what your mother was doing was unusual for for what what that average woman did in those days on the place?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I don't think she was doing anything. Average our neighbors was all the same way. Although the man was home with the neighbors. My mother's husband was gone, you see all that time. But then that was between them that she was willing to stay there and do these things because she could do it. And she had these, you know, we had sold eggs and butter and all of that stuff along with the other things. She didn't seem to think that she was working too. But she could do most of that. She could do all that by herself. She really didn't need to have a man do it for her. No, no, there was no man to do it. She had to do it. Because the dad was gone all the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Had she grown up on a farm?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I don't know if she had necessarily grown up on very much of a farm or folks lived in. Let's see, I would have believed it was. But I don't think she had. I think she worked out more than, you know, went to different homes and worked instead of doing other work. Until she was married.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did your parents meet? Do you know?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, my dad was from Missouri. And I really don't know where they met. But I imagine my mother was from Iowa. But I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah, well, it doesn't matter. I'm just thinking where they came from, you know. So how far from Kendrick was the home place?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Twelve miles… from here to up where we lived.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did she go into town very much?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, about once or twice a year. Drove a team. She could drive a team. My brother worked for the horses too, but then mother could do it the same as any of them. We rode horseback. We had two old horses. One would carry my mother and I, and the other one would carry two. Well, the one that mother rode. He was kind of a, he didn't like to have a second one on him. And he would raise quite a cohort around when we'd get on him. But that was just fun. As kids, we didn't think anything about it. We always had a horse or something to ride. And then when we'd come to town, usually mother would drive to town with a, oh, well, just anything they had in the house, a cart or something. Once in a while, we used to never have any snow to come to town. But once in a while we would get a, in February, we'd get snow. And we'd make a trip to town usually in February. My mother would come down, of course, in the fall now and all that and I'm heading my story. This, in February, we'd come to town and mother would get her a canning sugar. It was nearly always the cheapest in February. So she'd make her trips down here in February to get sugar. And I don't remember anything else but sugar. But of course, they bought their coffee, Arbuckle's coffee and Lion's coffee and all that they used to have. And then maybe kerosene, too. Yes, kerosene. We had a little store up on the ridge up there. He had a store and he carried all of his things mostly. He had a pack horse and then those pack boxes on the sides. And he would bring up coal oil and all that and we'd get our coal oil there. Or there mostly was where we took, oh, we'd take our eggs and things. But he'd take the eggs down there. Now he'd gather them eggs up and I guess he took them horseback. I don't remember any other way that he ever took a little horseback. And he'd bring those eggs down here then. When we sold them to him up there, we'd get our, oh, just different little things that we had to have. But we would put in quite a supply. Sometimes we'd send to Spokane and get a bill of some of the light coffee and macaroni and all of those extra things. We'd send Spokane for an order and get that. And then the other stuff was we would buy here in Kendrick. That is the biggest share of it. But we did send for a while. Then we'd send to Spokane to see what was the place. Bergens, I believe, was the name of the store. In Spokane we sent together.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And they would deliver it by mail? They would mail it down. So did you use the store on Cedar Creek very much?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yes, for all little things. And then once in a while he'd get, oh, maybe two or three bolts of calico or something like that. We'd get that there. And little things. We didn't get like a sack of sugar for a while. We never thought of getting it up there. But then we did come down here and get our sugar and flour and stuff down here, those bigger things.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you do much visiting when you came into Kendrick?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yes. We knew everybody in Kendrick. And, oh, I can't say now who all the people. But this Myron Long, we've known him ever since I was big enough to... Well, him and I were about the same age, but his folks were here. And they had the store. And then Myron carried it on for just... He's been out of this store now for maybe five years. But he had carried it on from his folks. They'd had it at Leland, and then they'd had it here. And then he carried it on for just a few years ago. And then he had to give it up. He's just a year younger than I am.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: By the way, did your folks ever say to you or give you an idea of why they finally picked around here to buy a place instead of somewhere else? What there was about Cedar Creek and Kendrick?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I don't know nothing in particular, only they were over in Montana, and they were in Kansas and in those different places. You know that sometimes they had a pretty hard time. And that is the people that lived there. And as they come out here, we lived down here for, I guess, a year, maybe before we went up there. And they looked around and they thought that that was a best looking and it happened to be that somebody, the people that we bought from, why they was wanting to get out, and we got a chance to get this place. And they were looking for a place and they finally decided that was it. And they liked everything as far as I know nothing in particular, only it was much better than any place that they ever been that they figured that they liked it. Maybe, I guess part of it, the difference is that the crops are a lot surer around here.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: I mean, you can count on them saying that. Well, we never had such a thing as a failure anywhere around here. And they were always very, well even today, the crops are just very good anywhere around. There's never been a, we had one wet year, oh that's been a good many years ago. But it didn't, we saved some of it. We saved enough to keep it going on. Well, not a lot of summer, we just worked out everything, but we never was. We never went hungry, I know that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, you know, you say that coming into town just a couple times a year, a year makes me think that it could be kind of lonely out there, but did you, was it?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, no, no, no. But then we made our own fun as far as being lonely. No, it was never lonely. We visited back and forth. We'd go and stay all night with one family, they'd all go and stay with one, then maybe next time the other family would come over to your place. And we did like that, and we had literary and dancing and popcorn. You know, time would all get together and pop popcorn and things like that. And oh, we made our own, what was never known in those days. We used to come horseback riding because I was too young. But my brother, my oldest brother, he used to come over to Texas Ridge from Cedar Creek. He'd come over to Texas Ridge to a dance or something like that. He'd come horseback riding. But while we'd go with a sled, if it was sledding time, we'd go with a sled from Cedar Creek over to South Lake in a sled. And that was a big deal. We'd take a big bobsled, you know, and everybody'd go together. And we'd know, we never... And Christmas, we had a big time Christmas, Christmas tree, and usually a program and a dance and everything, you know. And we had made our own entertainment. And then later years, different teachers came in there teaching, and then they would have plays, you know, different plays.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you play party games?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yes… yes, everything. All kinds of party games.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there a lot of kids that were within a few years of your age in the area?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yes… yeah, there was a bunch my age. And then my mother and, well, my mother and her friends was the ones that had all these parties and socials, you know. They had these basket socials and hard time parties, you know. Everybody dressed like they didn't have anything or something, you know. Oh, just entertainment. We had entertainment. We never thought of going in. I don't know when it was that I... I don't remember how old I was before I ever saw a picture show or anything like that. I thought the first time I was... Oh, I don't know. I'm just how old I must have been. In my 20s sometime, I had a baby or two, and I went to Milton, Oregon to visit my mother. She had moved down there. And I heard my first talking, the lady that she worked for took us over to Walla Walla. And the first... Well, I thought that was just something out of this world.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It was a talking movie?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: I can remember as well what I remember more than anything else was you saw this picture, this funny picture of those two birds, you know, that they're always around. They're crows, I think they were. And they were always around every place, you know. And they finally got... They was following somebody, going with somebody, and the little one got so he couldn't go, so he hops up on the other one. And I remember that as well as it was yesterday. And I just thought that was something. That little... was so cute, that I just thought it was just something out of this world.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they have actually talking in the film, or was it just a silent...

speaker: Frances Fry
words: It was a... Yeah. It was talking. That was the first one. And it was a... I'll tell you, it was a story. It always stayed in my mind how easy it could be that people very innocently could get into an awful mess and all of getting mixed up with somebody that got killed or something like that. And then they tried to lay it on to somebody, not the one that done it, but they tried to lay it on to them, see. And this was what that picture was about. And it was so easy that everything pointed to this one that they were trying to prosecute, but they didn't get to prosecute them. It had come out all right in the long run. But that was the first one that I ever heard or saw, you know. And it came out in this picture… and...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, when you were growing up, what were the kinds of things that you did that gave you, you know, enjoyment?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Living and... Oh, dancing and... ...living in Cedar. Riding horses and chasing cattle and all that stuff. I liked to ride. I liked to have... I always had a horse. And I liked to ride and do all that stuff. I did most... The boys, my two brothers, they went away to work. And I did quite a bit of the farm work, you know, plowing and taking care of the horses. I loved the outside. I would lots of other work outside than I would inside to come to work. I liked the outside work and I loved horses. Always did. I always had ponies, good ponies, to ride.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you still going to school when you were starting to help with plowing and farm work?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you do that like after you get home from school or would you lay out?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, Saturdays and Sundays if it was a busy time and steady time, I didn't make any difference.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were you using then? Were you using a foot burner?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Horses.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard it's not the easiest work to do, using a foot burner plow and getting it to go right.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, but if you're used to it, why it's all right, it's, you know... The only thing I couldn't do after I was married, I tried to run the binder, but I couldn't make it work. It would... Oh, I just had trouble with that, but I just... I could do most anything else. I could drive horses, I drove horses, I could drive two or four or anything like that, but I didn't make it go with the binder.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So at that point you were really... you must have been really used to your mother for you to be able to do that kind of work.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yeah, well, I just grew up with it. I just grew up with it and that was it. No, I liked the farm.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you stay in school there until the eighth grade? Did you go that... Then after that, what did you do? After you weren't in school anymore, did you stay at home and help?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, I was married when I was 18. And I had ten children.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you meet your husband right there in that area? Was he a local?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, he came from California. And his folks come up, they were wanting to get out of town. My grandmother was a... or his mother was a dressmaker. And she was working at that and his father was one of these traveling salesmen that he went and drove all of that. That's when they just had buggies and like that. They drove all over the country and took orders and brought in things. They had their... like when they had a hotel here, why they had a sales room and he'd bring his stuff there, you know, and show it in these different places where he'd go. And he was that and she... and this boy, he was... he was about 20, I guess, or 21. And him and his brother was with the mother. And then they had hired Elf. And they had a ranch, or had this ranch, and they had raised cattle and done numerous things like that. But they come in, they had the money to just come in and buy what they wanted. That was pretty unusual for somebody to have that money just come in. Yes, at that time it was. It was very unusual because anybody that... most of them had... you know, there's just... the man died several years ago and the woman is up in the home, Moscow. A friend of ours that was raised right there on the ridge when I was and all, why they lived right there all the time. And so she just had to be... she was put in this on daddy as they put her in the home up there. And she's been in there, but she was older than I was. And she'd lived her life there too, but she's still alive. But there's not very many of us that's left anymore.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, when you...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: where did you meet your husband? Do you remember? Huh? Do you remember how you...

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Not especially, no. We just had these parties and we'd go to these parties. And that's all it was. We just had the parties and then we finally decided to get married. So that was it. And then my mother was a widow then for a good many years. But she moved then down. My brother, older... or my middle brother lived down at Milton Freewater and she went down there for a good many years. Then my youngest brother lives at Spokane now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, when you married, did you... where did you move to?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: We went and lived with his mother on there for one place.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did you feel that when you got married then, did you need to have very much to set up a house keeping?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No. We didn't need to have to have... We didn't need it and we didn't have to have... Well, just a lot of things. But the kids nowadays, my gosh, they have to have it all before they ever get married. But we didn't. We just worked into it as we could and that's all there was to it. And sometimes it seemed like it was pretty hard with the children, so many of them. Then we got by with it and they all turned out to be just average kids. They all went to high school and they've all done pretty well. I've got them all pretty close around. It's like we lost one girl, well, we lost a baby, and then we lost this girl when she was 13. But otherwise, I had the rest of my children just all around the country here close enough that we all get together every once in a while, them and their families.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The girl that died when she was 13, what did she die of?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: She had what they call lady cancer, sarcoma or lady cancer.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, when you were married then, did you do much work besides raising the family in those first years?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yes, I worked outside in the field. I helped my husband until my boys were 12 years old. I helped him shock grain and done anything he wants to do. I took care of most of it. I took care of the cattle. We had milk cows and I sold cream and all that stuff. I took care of all that. Then I would shock the grain and all… i don't know… i don't know how I'd done it all, but I did. It just seems like I'm really interested in this because it seems like so many women would have preferred to stay inside and take care of the house. I've known some women who said they liked to get outside and work, but you're probably the first person I've known that really went out and did it. I worked out until my boys were 12 years old. Then when they were 12 years old, I said, I'm not going out anymore. Of course, I had a girl. By that time, the girls knew how to work. Every one of my girls can work. They can cook and do everything just better than I can. But we all worked together in that way. When I went outside to work, I would plan what the girls were to do, and they would do the housework and the cooking after they got to be, I guess, ever since they were maybe six, eight years old. Every one of them can cook. Even my boys, every boy can cook, of God. Oh, yes, and then we used to butcher our own meat, and I made my soap, and we rendered the lard. I rendered just many gallons and gallons of lard, and I sold the lard. I made butter. Milk cows made butter. I sold cream, and all of that stuff all went along with everything else and my canning. But people won't believe when I tell them what I canned, what I used to can. I never thought of canning. My fruit was all after the children got any size at all. Well, my fruit was all in a half a gallon jar. Of course, I wouldn't make dates for them, so I'd have to can my fruit. And we would get six and seven hundred pounds of tomatoes and peaches and, let's see, potatoes and peaches and prunes. I made just prune butter and apple butter and stuff like that.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: People make little jars of it now. I made it by the gallons, just by the gallons. Well, we had to have it that way. The children all liked it, and we liked that one. We were just eating that. And then after I was on the farm, my husband used to take our wheat, you know. We took it down to Potluck, and we'd get our winter's supply of flour. And I, for a long, long, many, many years, I made one sack of flour. I'd make up in a week's time in bread. We ate that, one sack of flour made up into bread in a week's time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now, how much was in a sack? That would be forty -nine pounds?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, fifty pound sacks. And I made bread, and of course, I would cook a main cake and all that stuff besides. But the bread was the main thing that I had to use that flour for.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now, in a week's time?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: In a week's time. Now, that's hard to believe, but I did it for many, many, many months. Not only weeks, but years, you might say. I used a fifty pound sack of flour a week. And we would take our wheat down and change it for flour down at Potluck. There was a mill down there. We took it down there, and we'd get our wheat and our oats and our different stuff for mush, you know, and like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Okay, now fifty pound sack, how much of that would go to bread?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, the main part of it went to bread. Yeah, because I would, what wasn't anything, I, well, usually on Saturdays, I baked anywhere from, oh, from, no, I won't say for sure, but I baked anywhere from ten to twelve loaves of bread on Saturdays. Well, I baked three times a week. So you know what that took. It was no small amount. And then we had meat. We took care of our own meat. We butchered it. And for a long, long time, we never canned beef. But finally, we got to where we butcher beef. It wasn't anything. We butchered after the family got any size at all. We butchered nine hogs at a time and then cut it up, you know, and took care of it, made it into hams and bacon. And then I, well, we used to can, I used to can all the pig's feet and all head cheese and all that stuff. I made that up. And then I'd have that to you, which you know, through the year. And we had meats of all kinds of bacon and ham and shoulder all through the summer. We'd smoke it, you know, then put it in sacks, hang it out. We had a, a, a greenery out in the barn, new greenery. And we'd put that in sacks and hang it out there in this greenery. It was cool in there all the time. It was a big barn, you know, big, big barn. And that's where we hung that meat and kept it all, all year.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the beef? Did you salt it?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, we didn't for long. No, I canned that. When they were, when I got to, finally we got to killing a beef. Later years, there was an old Dutchman that come from Germany. He used to stay at our place quite a little bit. And he was a real butcher. And there was nothing went to waste. When he'd done the butchering, there was nothing went to waste. He made everything into the cup to meat. And we got barrels, big wooden barrels. And he put his, this, the, oh, hams and shoulders and meat all down in the barrel and made the brine and put over it. And he'd let it go so long. And he used to go, he had a homestead over there pretty close to where we lived later years. And he'd come in and go back in the cellar where we kept the barrels. He'd go back in there and he'd just swish his hand down in the barrel like that and come up. And it'd be either it was all right or he had to take it out and hang it up and let it drain. And he re -et that stuff and then put it back on the meat. We did that for years. And there wasn't anything. He made everything. He made liverwurst and blood sausage. And all kinds of stuff, you know, sausage and stuff like that. And tripe, when we booked your beef, then he made the tripe. I don't know whether you know anything about that or not, but we had that too. So we had everything in the meat line to eat like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He would just be able to tell from running his hand through the brine?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, he could just come right in and just swish his hand down. That's the way you do it. And he would feel of it and there was a feeling or something that then had to be taken out. Well, then he just took it all out and hung it up in the smokehouse and let it drain while he got this. Would re -heat this, you know, and everything and get it ready to cook.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was he working as a hired hand for you during this time?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, no.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He was staying with you?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: He'd just come over and stay and sometimes he'd come over and we'd like to come over and eat meals with us. You know, he was alone.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He was a bachelor?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yes, and he would milk the cows and different things like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He had a place that he was homestead?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: He had a little homestead up there, yes. Later years, for a while he did, but for later years he had a little homestead and he'd stay over there and then he'd come over. Mox Herzog was his name. Well, you were saying about the canning.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did you get all these, all the peaches and prunes from? Much of that grown right there?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yes. There was a lot of it grown and then we bought the peaches and tomatoes. We'd go down to Juliaetta here and buy the tomatoes and then we'd get our peaches wherever we could. You used to get them down to Louis and you'll get them with a 50 pound box or if you went down to... We never went to the orchards very often and got them, but we could get them at times. The end of the week we could get them. But then we did go a lot of times too, down to before they took them orchards all out along the little Louis down there. We used to go down there and get them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Give me an idea of how much you would can a year. You haven't really said that, of that stuff. Like how many cans of peaches and tomatoes?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I would get... Oh, I don't know if I can tell you. Hundreds of pounds I'd buy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Of each one?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yes. And you could kind of go with that as far as... I know it was just... Well, it was just tables and tables when I was canning it. It was just tables and tables. And we had a fruit room on the ranch. And I had... Well, there was five or six and there was four. They'd go four side and side, four in the shelf. And then I just had rows and rows of them. Peaches and pears and tomatoes and then plums and apple sauce. You know, the fresh apple sauce. You put a green apple sauce and all like that. I just canned. Well, just hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of corks. I don't know. Just what it'd be. Boy, that sounds like an awful lot. And then later years we had the cherry orchard up there too on Cedar Creek. And I canned lots of cherries. Oh, I've often wondered what some of these women... After they got to having the... We used to have the thrashers. The men would come in with the teams and bundle wagons and everything. They'd move in on us with the old steam thrashers and they'd be there for days. One year we had the beans. It'd come a bad year. And they'd be there maybe one day and get the thrash and the next day it'd rain. And I had the bean thrashers for three weeks. And they'd come and go. And then the boys would go a lot of times when they were there. It was hunting time. They could go get birds and things. So they'd go get birds and I'd fix the birds for their eats and stuff. And like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And you fed them off and on for three whole weeks?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: They would come and go because the machine had come in from over on the Potlatch. And when they left our place, they went over to our neighbor's. Of course we had quite a big place there where we were that they could wash and like that. And when they went over to the neighbor's, it had rained over there a little bit. And when it rained over there, they'd come over to my house.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: To get the eats?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yes. And we used to have a good time. But then they were all kind of neighbor boys. Not only were they not really neighbor boys because they would have had to go quite a ways to go home. And these people were kind of funny folks anyway. And even when it was cold, you know, it was getting cold in the fall with the beans. And they wouldn't even let them in the house hardly to wash or anything. Well they just... Our house was just a house that they could come to and come in. We had an extra big long room there that you could back. No, I'm going back. And then they'd come in there and set up this big fire, big stove, you know, big pot bellied stove they called them I guess. There's a long one. Now go on back. She can't hear but she can see me. And they'd come over there and sit. During the day if it was, they could work at these other parts. Oh just, we had lots of good times. Of course the kids nowadays wouldn't think it was very good but we used to have lots of good times with all these...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: With the neighbors?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: With the neighbors and like that or whoever happened to be there if the crashing crew was there. Well, it was... Well in those days what was it when you say good times and it would be different than what the kids would think it would be today.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was good times just visiting then?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, we'd visit or play cards or oh just most anything just sit and visit and then have a big meal. And you'll have to excuse me for just a few minutes while I put my dog on. Go on. Dinners go on well. Lots of times maybe this year they'd be a bunch come to our place and wasn't anything for us to have. Of course there was quite a few of our own family and then the neighbors 30 or 40 was no job at all. We just had a big dinner.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: At your place?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yes, and then we had for many many many years we had an Easter dinner over wherever the place... It would be according to what the weather was and we'd go over and have a big Easter dinner over where the sawmill was. And one time we was over there and had a big Easter dinner and we could have our Easter dinner down in the lower part. And then we had toboggans and stuff and there was a hill there that we could come down you know toboggan on the hill. The snow was crusted and all and we could ride on that. That was at Easter time one year. Of course it wasn't every year. Things like that. We had big sleigh parties and stuff like that too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: These big dinners were they unusual or were they often done?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, no we had them every once in a while. We'd go to one house and then to another and we'd go for a surprise on somebody maybe for an evening of dancing and like that. And we'd go you know and maybe sometimes they'd try to fool them and just come you know on them unexpected and things like that. And lots of times we'd go and dance and dance all night and have breakfast then go home… things like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who would be the given music on the dancing?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well we had several in the neighborhood that could play the violins and whatever they happened to have. A harp, a mouth organ we'd dance to sometimes when we didn't have anything else.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What kind of music did they play?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well violin and... Well I mean the kind of stuff that they kind of songs that they would play was the old fashioned. Just the real old fashioned music.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: After you were married and had children did this still continue?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh yeah… we'd take our kids and we had a place especially fixed at our hall, our central, the schoolhouse. It was an upstairs to the schoolhouse that we had for the dancing hall. And we had a place there and put our babies down when there wasn't anybody to leave them with. Grandma was at my house a good share of the time and mine was big enough that I could leave them. Well I'd just leave them when they weren't. Well I took them with me. Everybody else did the same.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So some dances were at the school and some dances were at people's homes?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah. Excuse me… bad times too but then nothing. Nothing so bad that... Each neighbor helped the other one. If somebody was sick while my mother used to go and help the neighbors, great deal. And she would be called out any time day or night while she was going to help the neighbors. I helped a lot of my neighbors when I was up there too. We just kind of depended on one another. That was the way it went.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were some of the bad times that you're thinking of?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh nothing in particular, only sickness or something like that. We never thought of a doctor. We just do it yourself. You had to do what there was. If you thought you were doing right, that was it. It's very seldom we ever went to a doctor. Or anything. We just think, well we had this or that or something else.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What could you do in the case of sickness if you went to somebody's house to try to help them? What kind of could you do? I mean you didn't have any medicine of the type that the doctors would prescribe?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, that the doctors would give but we'd have different... Each household had different things that they used. Some would use one thing and some would use something else. And then we'd do the best we could with what we had. Just pass it out to whoever was sick. But sometimes it was just colds and sometimes it was the mother that was sick. And sometimes it was someone else that she needed help from. Like that. We just helped one another.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there tuberculosis in the area at all that you knew of?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No… some places had it kind of bad. Yes, I know there were several on our ridge that had passed away with it. But at my time that I was up there I don't know of anybody that had it. But before I was around like that very much there was one or two that passed away on our ridge. Of course there's some of the girls of my Welsh. There's a lady now that she's still alive. She's in her 80s. She was a neighbor and her mother died with... Her mother died though with a childbirth. And then she was the oldest one in the family. That is the oldest girl. And then there was a brother older than she was. And the grandfather had died with tuberculosis and this boy took it and he died with tuberculosis. Well that was during the time that we were younger people up there because she was taking care of the family. Then everybody would go and help if they'd get down and were sick and had to have someone to be with them at night or something like that. Why people would just take turns and go and stay. Each neighbor would... Maybe I'd go one night and they'd go another night and somebody else would go some other night.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: And then in those days why? When anybody passed away why? The neighbors would all go in and help. And there was usually one or two that could take care of the bodies. And we'd set up at night, you know, somebody to stay there all night. And then we'd bury them. I don't know, we never had to.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You mean just the next day?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, or two. Never could go over more than about two days. And now they have to have thousands of dollars to bury you. But people, there was some people up there that made it. Made the boxes and casket and everything. Fixed it, which is nice as anything… we never..… but there was people in the neighborhood that did that work, you know, would do those things. And there was people that would... We had a lady there that would always go when those babies come. They'd always go to anybody's house that was there and needed it. Why, they'd always go and help with them. For years and years they never had a doctor. Just one of the women would go, or two.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there one or two women who knew, especially about midwifing? They were the ones that did it? The same women would always go?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, they would always go. They'd call on when my first baby came. Why, I asked this old lady, she had always been, that's all we knew. This lady always went and helped the different ones. So when I asked her if she'd come over to my house, she said yes. She said she would, but she says I want you to have a doctor. But then she says I'm getting older, and she said it bothered her, but she says I'll come and be with you. And so she'd come.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you have a doctor then?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Then we had a doctor too. But she insisted on me having a doctor. She said that she thought it was best. But never to my notion did they ever lose any babies when she took care of them. And she took care of a grandson of hers. My Landy was only about that long. But she took care of him and raised him. He's still alive. He worked at the university for a long time. I don't know if he's still up there or not.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, in those days, was it okay for the mother to work right up until she gave birth?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: As long as she could go, that was all there was to it. But this thing was then why you were supposed to stay in bed nine days afterwards.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Long time.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, they were supposed to then. And mine, when they got to, well, that baby one day and the next day they're up going, walking. Things like that. Well, I don't know. It just seemed like it wasn't too bad.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember the flu?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yeah… my whole family was down with the flu. I had, I got it, I think I had it first. And then I just got to where I could kind of be around when the rest of my family took it. Let's see what it was about. And that was Grandma, Clancy's mother, she was there. Then my mother lived up across the hill from Oslo, it always, and she had my youngest brother. And she came down to help me. Well, then the brother took it. And she would come down and help me with the children. I was alone. Mr. Fry took a notion he'd go hunting with a bunch of men. We didn't want him to go, but he went anyway. So he didn't anymore and get gone. And then he wasn't any good around sick people anyway. And he hadn't been gone for a day or two. We sent for him. And told him he had to come home. So he came home and he'd come home all right. But he wasn't home and there too, he was down in bed. So it was just my mother and I then that took care of the whole bunch of them. But I had taken it first. I had already got that as I was over it to a certain extent. But then I had to go ahead. There was nobody else to go ahead but my mother. And so I took my turn with her and she'd go back and forth to her place. But she'd come back and stay nights and like that. And then we had her boy then took her. You know, my brother. He took her. So he was there. So I had that whole bunch there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you do? How did you take care of them with the flu?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I just took care of them. Besides, the neighbors will come in. They didn't come in the house. They wouldn't come in the house, any of them. But they come over and took care of the stock. We had a bunch of stock and they just come in and they said they'd do anything outside or anything that was to do to milk the cows or feed the stock or anything like that. They did all of that. The neighbors come and go. But then my mother and I took care of all of these that were sick. Some of them was quite sick. Some of them wasn't too bad. We took care of them anyway. My mother never did take it. Quite a few people died from that flu. Oh, yes. I know there was. Some of the healthiest and most healthy people that you ever saw. They was going to wear it out, but they didn't make it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Wear it out?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, they said they'd wear it out. They died.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did they mean by that?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, they just wasn't careful or didn't try to take care of themselves. They just died. But they wasn't... Well, I don't know anyone that died with the flu up on our ridge, but there was a lot of them that was awful sick. And it took them an awful long time to get over it. It was the after effects if you didn't take care of yourself. It was the elements and all. You'd take it again and then you was gone. That's what happened to several of them because they wouldn't take care of themselves. They'd just go out in the air and think it was spinning. Think they was all right and just go out and that was it. There were just quite a few we knew of that, but we didn't have any bad effects. And it took a long time. And Clarence and his mother both, that was my husband and his mother. They were more of a...

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, I don't know. It seemed like when they got anything it was always worse than anybody else had. So they were harder to take care of than all a bunch of kids as far as that was concerned.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You think they might have had to do with the fact that they'd had an easier... It sounds like they had an easier life. I mean, if they had money and had done pretty well for themselves, they were maybe used to it.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: I don't know something of that sort, but they weren't well. They were more apt to, just like after my husband got over it. There were just lots of times that I would be working taking care of the children and all. When I was weak, and I would, oh, you know, perspire and feel so weak and bad. Well, he commenced complaining after he was up for a while. Well, he commenced complaining on the same thing. And I said, well, I said I had that just the same, but I would work it off to a certain extent. But I didn't do no extensive work, no more than what I had to, because I didn't dare to. Because I knew I was the one that had to be the head there, because that was just what I had to do. That was all. But it seemed like my family was more of a... more stable. They were stronger in a way you might say, I guess.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: When things were tough. And they were more, oh, I don't know. They didn't think... they done the best they could, and that is all they could do. But sometimes the others didn't do what they should have.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I've seen in some families where it seems to me like the woman really does more than the man does. I mean, he kind of leans on her and lets her do it, almost as if she's mothering him.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I know that was great, but I couldn't get the way it was at our place, because he would say I can't do it. Well, when it had to be done, somebody had to do it. That's all it was to do it. So I'm not bragging at all, because it was just... I was able to do it and I did it. I know a lot of people, oh, they bring you out of bed when I had to take care of all of them, because I had just got over it myself. That is, was getting over. And they said, well, they were just... and they all looked for me to get down again, but I didn't. But with my mother's help, if it hadn't been for my mother, I couldn't have made it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you have to do to take care of them when they were down? I mean, would you just have to bring their food?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yes, carry their food and just take care of them, just like you would if they did anything. They just had to be watched after. You know, this kind of outside work that you did, I'd like you to tell me a little about what the actual farming would be.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: There were certain times in the year that you would have to do a get out and do quite a bit on the farm?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yeah… harvest and all like that, and when you were busy. And I've run the mower and a lot of those things. One fall we had to take and our clover was short. I drove the team and Mr. Fry walked behind and it was so short that we had to rake that over so that we could get it. And he would walk and get it and I rode that. And boy, I don't know how cold it was because I know we just pretty near froze. It was just that cold working, trying to get that. We had the plowing in the spring while we had the working of the alfalfa was the first thing. I always used to feel so sorry for the horses because that was rough work on the horses, was this taking care of the alfalfa. You had to take these spring tooth hairs, you know what they are. Well, you had to hook your horses onto them and it was a constant. And nearly every horse would have a sore shoulder from that beating over there. The ground would be really rough. It would be rough and hard and this would be a digging kind of clawed up. And that was the hardest work for the horses to do.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you do that work? Would you take the teams?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, no I never worked at that. But I did rake hay and the hay was up. I used to rake hay and I helped to shock it. And he tried to get someone to help him, you know, besides me when he put it in the barn because he had a hay fork, you know. That was when they had first had the hay forks and got it up into the barn. And then someone in the barn had smoothed it around while the other fellow was forking it up. And then there was usually one of the kids that run the horse that had a horse on this hay fork. But they did that at that time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did you shock hay then?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, we had it in bundles and you had to stand it up, you know, make it into shock. There was a lady come from Canada. She came down and our boys, they weren't grown and they were just good sized boys. And the two of them was out shocking for their dad. Their dad was earning the binder and she called it stooking. And it just like the tickled our kids. She says, oh you're stooking. And of course they didn't know what she meant. We laughed about it afterwards. She was an ultra nice person and we finally told her about it. They thought it was so funny. They said they were stooking.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I'll tell you, it's just hard for me to see how you could raise a family, do all the inside work, put up all the fruit and do all the cooking, and do so much of the outside work too. I just find that, it sounds like what for today would be a job for two people.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I sometimes wonder myself how I've done it, but I did it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you? What?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, my girls and when they got big enough they did. But I didn't let them do much of that canning. But I'll tell you, I had a, well we had a good friend that was Billy Myers. He was the blacksmith man over here. He used to live here in town. And he had the blacksmith. And I used to have a boiler. I used to boil my fruit, would set it in, you know, fix it and put it in the jars and set it in the boiler and boil it. And I never would let the children, the girls touch it because I was afraid they'd get it. So this man, he'd come to our place a lot. So he went to work and he made galvanized, all that thick galvanized stuff like that. And he made me a canner. And I could put, let's see, I think it was, let me see. I believe it was 30 jars in that. I'd put that on my stove. It'd cover the top of my stove practically. And I would put that on there and then put my fruit in there. And I could take that much at a time. I could fill my jars and get them ready and put them in there. Well, then when it come to come off, why I had to just slide it back and then take the lid off and let it cool before I took it out because it was hot. I didn't want to bother with it unless it was too hot. And that's the way I can just lots and lots and lots of fruit. When you say slide it back, you left the canner right on the stove. You didn't pull it off. You just took the top off. Took the top off and slid it back as far as I could. So there was a, you know, there used to be, oh, on the stoves they had, you know, those that had water in them. Yeah, yeah. There was an extra. That was that much extra on the stove, you know, on the back. And you could slide it over enough that I could go ahead then on the front and do my cooking and have this back enough to leave it so I could get to it and then get the jars out then. Wash them, see, most all of them at that time we used those Mason jars, you know, and you'd have to put your rubbers would be on there and your lids would be on. And then you'd put them in there and you'd tighten them down. And then when you took them out, well, then you'd have to see that they were tied and then set them out to cool. And then my berries, I canned them the same way. And, oh, we had berries to pick and all that stuff. We had the garden and everything besides. I used to can beans. I never made no success a can of peas. So I said I'd scrub floors before I tried to can them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why is that?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: I could not keep them. Lots of people can can them, but I couldn't keep them. They just wouldn't keep them for me. And so I would just...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, the one thing I'm wondering about with the outside work and the farming is, did you do that because you wanted to or because you felt you had to? Or because your husband wanted to?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: I did more or less because I felt we had to. We couldn't hire anybody else. And then when my girls got big enough, why they would... I would plan the meals and they'd fix the meals and I'd go out and work my field.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This is just work that was more than your husband could possibly do by himself?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, he couldn't do it. No. Unless he could... And we didn't have the money to hire a gun. So I just done it.

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: Hi, mama.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Now what's your name?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Sam. Sam Schroeder. Sam Schroeder. I work for the county museum.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: I necessarily had to, but I did do it. There was nothing... I never thought of anything else. Because he couldn't do it by himself.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what about taking care of the livestock? Is that something he could have done if you didn't want to do it?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: You did take care of the livestock. Well, he took care of the horses, but I took care of the cows and the pigs. Along with my work. Did all the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did some families hire people whereas you didn't have the money to do that?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, they could hire them. And lots of times they did. And in those days, lots of times that fellow would come and maybe stay the winter. It just frees bored. If you furnished him for his eats and his bed and like that, he'd come over in the winter for nothing.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you do that? Have people stay?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Because he could do that in the winter. He didn't ask what to do. But then a lot of people did. Once in a while we had some around, but then we never had to. Because I was so I could do... If anything happened, I could take care of it. Everything was just as well as he could. So the horses and cows and everything was concerned. I did that too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, comparing what your family did to the neighboring families, do you think that you put up a lot more, did a lot more canning and that sort of thing than most of the families did?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Most of the families on the ridge at that time did the same thing. They canned lots of things too. We'd go pick berries on the shares. And give them... We would pick them and give them so many for the berries. And then we'd bring them home and get them when we didn't have them. Things like that. No, no, we had... I don't think there was any... I don't think we had a neighbor. We had a neighbor up there. But if you needed something, all you had to do was to say something. Because your neighbor would come and help you. And the same way with you. So if they needed you, you'd go to them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You would go of your own initiative?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh yeah. If they needed help or we thought they needed help or they were sick or anything like that, well we'd go help them. And they'd do the same way with us.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there any times when a family would just be in such bad shape financially that they would need help, that they would need food or clothes?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well we had one family that came up there on the ridge that they just borrowed. And what was the worst of it was, they had quite a few children. And he wouldn't work at all hardly. And they'd send the children to beg for something. And finally he just kept it up for so long. And he rented several different places. And he wouldn't even get out and get, you know, most any place you can get some wood. And he wouldn't get out and get any. He'd tear some maybe off of a wood shed or off of the barn or something. He'd tear some boards and things off of that and burn it instead of fixing it for himself. So we got tired of that pretty quick. So they were the only family though that I know of. Well it was families I know that was hard up. I have talked to a lady here not too long ago that she raised a big family up there too. And they didn't have too much. And then she helped another family. She was talking about it when I talked to her. She was real old. And when I talked to her she was telling about how good she thought everybody was up there. And then she told about this one family. And she said, well, she said she knew that sometimes she didn't have too much. But she said she knew sometimes that this other lady had quite a family. And she would give her things, you know, things like that. And she says, I know that she needed it. I knew she needed it. And things like that. But she helped her anyway. Yeah, she helped her. Well if anybody was in need or anything, we'd maybe get up a party or we'd take up something or give something to them. And I don't mind helping people that will try to help themselves. But when they don't help themselves, I've not got no use for them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you say have a party, you mean you might throw a party for the family?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yes, or something like that. And people bring things in or give something. Or they'd give, well, in the fall maybe they'd say, well now you come over. And if they had potatoes or anything. Now we went over to our neighbors a good many times. He lost his wife. So I used to go over and he loved to have old pine cake and things like that. And I'd go over and maybe spend a day and a half over there. And I'd bake cake and fix everything for him to eat, you know, and bake him bread. Because he was used to having that and like that. Well, he always raised lots of nice rutabagas and turnips and potatoes and all of that stuff. Well, then we'd go over and help him take that in, take his garden in. Well, then when we got ready to go home, he'd give us all we wanted. Well, we didn't have a garden.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he have any children?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No… it was just him and his wife. And his wife passed away, but they were good neighbors. They were lovely neighbors. But I don't know of anybody up there that wasn't a good neighbor. I don't know of anybody.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This one family that was kind of mooching off people.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: This one family, they were just, well, they bragged on, they knew how much they could get from the time they left the East to coming out this way. At the different places they could stop and wear their welcome out there. And the officers had to just come and pick them up up there and take them away.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is that would finally happen to them?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah… and I know this lady went, one day she went over to one of these people and she went with the boy that day. And he went over and she wanted some potatoes and she wanted this and she wanted that. So the man, it was just him and his wife, they were alone, they were old. They were alone, but they had a garden and stuff. So he went out and she had walked over there. And he went out and he had a little buggy with a team. So he took a sack of potatoes and oh, he took, well, practically everything that she needed. And she told her, or he told her and I said, I'll take you home. So he took her home and she said, they was always saying they'd pay it back and they'd pay it back. He says, no, he says, you don't need to pay it back. He says, I've given you these things. He says, I don't, you don't need to pay it back. But he says, don't come back anymore.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: That's it… but they'd send, he wouldn't go himself. He'd just sit around, wouldn't go. And they'd send the little children up to the neighbors. They could get all the milk they wanted if they'd just go up to this one place and it wasn't very far. And do you think he'd go up there? No, he'd send the kids. And they got tired of that too. So I told my husband, I said, well, I said, I'm not going to give them anything more. I said, if the children come up here, I'll feed them. But I said, I'm not going to send nothing. I said, they can get out and get something.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I take it they were just renting and they didn't own it all. Is that why they finally got kicked out? Because they weren't paying their rent?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, they didn't pay rent. They didn't do anything that was bothering anybody. And then he was one of these fellows that, well, the neighbors up there, if you was, if you happened to be walking to town or walking someplace or anything, they'd pick you up. You know, that was when they had a car, that is a pickup or car or something. Well, they always had asked the neighbors to ride with them. Well, one time these boys was coming down the road and this fellow was walking. And no, they picked him up. He was on his way home and they picked him up. And when he went to get out of the pickup or a rig, when he went to get out, he stumbled. And he didn't fall, but he stumbled. And he turned around and he says, well, it's a good thing that I didn't fall and hurt myself. He says, I just hurt you. Now that's the kind of fellow he was. So we kind of commenced to kind of steer around. But that's the only one. There was people up there, quite a few people up there that lived that didn't have too much. But maybe if I went over to someplace and I had an extra supply of something, I'd take them something. Well, then if they had an extra supply of something, they'd bring me something or they'd take something to somebody else. We always had a little extra that we could divide with our neighbors. We never were so hard up with what we could, you know, could each have a little something. And that's the way we did.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you, in something like that, did you try to figure what your neighbor might need or did they have to say to you what they needed?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, they never was. They were neighbors that would ask you or let you even know. They didn't want you to really know. But then you could tell when you'd go, we'd visit one another all the time. And you could tell, well, if they was out of this or they was out of that or they were out of something else. Well, maybe the next time, why we went, why we took, if we had a supply, we took it. And that's the way they all did. Each one helped the other.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And it wasn't something that anybody would keep track of what you owed or something like that? Or it wasn't something that mattered this year? I mean, it could be years from now that they might help you.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, you could. Well, but then we were all kind of in the same boat. So they would all do the same thing. If we needed something, well, we'd get it. That is, if any of them found it out, well, we'd get a help doing it and things like that. Just like I started to tell you about this man that used to come to my mother's there to help her when dad was gone all the time. And he'd come over there and help her. And at the end of the year, every year, it didn't make any difference whether they had a dime or didn't have a dime. They'd always, my dad and him, would always figure out, they put down everything through the years when something was, if he worked, you know, and did something special, my dad was supposed to pay him for. Then if dad got him something, my dad would pay for it. And then at the end of the year, they would always straighten up their books. They would always get their books straight. Sometimes they'd owe one, sometimes they'd owe the other, but they had these books straight every year.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He would actually put in the crop for your father. Yeah. He would put it in and he would harvest it too. And your father would pay him for his work.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: And then one year they logged a little bit. Oh, just different little things like that that he'd done that my dad couldn't do or didn't do. But they'd always had their books and they'd put it down. They knew just what it was and then when it came to... Because my dad didn't know anything about farming when he went up there on Cedar Creek. They'd talk about the single trees and double trees and all of that stuff, you know. This fellow they had what they call an evener. Well, it's a long piece of timber. Maybe you know what they are. I think I do, but... Well, there's a short end and a long end. Well, they put the one horse on the long end and put two horses on the short end. That's what they call an evener. And these fellas, they didn't know why this one old horse couldn't keep up. Because they'd put her on the evener end and she was working against the other two. We used to laugh about that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who did that? Was that your father?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: My dad.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he learn eventually?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Oh, yes he did. Then he used to, in the early day too, you know, it was hard to buy shells and all that stuff for your gun. And there was lots of birds in the fall. There was lots of young birds, you know, he'd feed and like that. Well, my dad always would pick up old little rocks about that big. He'd always have his pocket full of rocks. And these birds that fly up in the tree, he could pick a bird out of a tree with a rock just easier and you could shoot it almost. That way he saved his 22 shells instead of using them for birds. He could use that for something else and he had these rocks and he could knock them out of there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were those grouse and pheasants?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Grouse and pheasants.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That sounds pretty slick to me.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, it was slick. And at that time they were so plentiful that they weren't scared to death like they are now. You can't hardly get near one now, you know, because there's a few of them that you can't hardly get near. But in those days they'd hop up there and be up there in the trees. We'd all be looking to see where they were, you know, and then finally he'd locate them. Boy, he'd get up and then my boys got to doing that. One of my boys could throw a rock pretty good. He was a pretty good shot.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, was there a church on Cedar Creek too? Any kind of church that you had?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: No, not for a long, long time. There was no church there. They would have services maybe at somebody's house or something like that. There's a church up there now and it's been there for quite a while. Or they'd have a church or schoolhouse. But they didn't have a regular church. And when they did it was a non -denominational.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Denominational?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah… anybody could go and everybody was welcome to come, whoever came in there to preach a sermon or anything like that. I know that we had quite a fight after we got to church up there. There was quite a fight going on in the neighborhood about having dances. Some people were just so against dancing and all like that. Some of the ministers are against it too. But there was one minister that they all pretty well liked, just real good. They'd always have a harvest ball. After the harvest was all over, we'd have a great big dance. And we'd have a Christmas, maybe a Christmas ball or something like that. Well, one time this fellow came over and he was to preach. And they were having what they called protracted meetings. They used to go out and stay for weeks. And one fellow said, somebody said to him, how long was it going to last?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: And he said, well, he didn't know, I guess, as long as the eats were left. And things like that. Well, this minister said to the boys, now he knew who the boys were that were giving. There was a certain number would give a dance at one time and then some other time and then someone else would give a dance. He went to these boys and I said, boys, I'll tell you what I'll do. He says, if you'll all come over and listen to my preaching, he says, I'll start a half hour, an hour early. And you all come over and listen to me. And then he says, then you can go over and have your dance. And he says, if I wasn't a minister, that is, I wasn't supposed to be a minister. He said, I wouldn't mind going over too. But he says, that isn't the way I can do. But he says, I'll have my meetings. And you know, there was everybody went to that church and went to his over what?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: They went, we went over and had our dance. The harvest ball. Yeah, well, I don't know if it was that harvest ball, but they were having those protracted meetings anyway at the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, it's kind of funny that some people would get opposed to dancing if it had been going on in the neighborhood for so long. And from what you say, they'd always had dancing in the neighborhood.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, we always had dances, but then they had their church too, but then they didn't all go to church. I know that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But this not liking dancing kind of grew in the church when they built the church.

speaker: Frances Fry
words: They tried every way they could to, you know, to keep them from dancing, but then they didn't. The neighborhood, why they'd be from Southwick and from what we call Boulder Creek and all around there, why they'd be people come from miles to our dances up there. We had big dances, everybody.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Those would be in the school mostly? Those would be at the school, the dances?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: But not… and things like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And you had a second floor, you said, in the school for dancing?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, they had the upstairs for dancing. It still stands up there, the schoolhouse, and they're using the lower part of it. They've kind of fixed it up. And we have our pioneer picnic the last Sunday of this month. Why, we have a primary picnic, and we've been wanting to get that fixed so they could have it up there, but they haven't had it. They had it down at Clarkston for many years, and last year or two years, they've had it over here at the fire hall. And all the old pioneers that's around are supposed to come. So that's come up now. I don't know for sure whether they'll have it this year or not, but they'll have it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is Cedar Creek what they call the neighborhood? Is that what they call the neighborhood?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Yeah, it's the Cedar Creek neighborhood. And there was Park, and there was Crescent, and Southwick, and all those little places around there. But we all congregated together. We had lots of people come from those other places, too. And they went, a lot of people went to them. A lot of times these fellows that played for our dancers up there played for these other dancers, too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Meetings, what I would call revivals, is that what they were?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, some of them. But then some of these were the things that they go and have their tents, you know, have their big tents. And everybody goes and maybe stays nights, they'll have it for a week or so. And they'll take their, who used to, go and have these protracted meetings or revivals or whatever they, I don't know what to call them now. Then they used to always go, and then people would go and come that was close enough. They'd go and come, but they always took eats. You know, always, everybody took, donated their eats. And everybody would go and take all their kits and everything. That was a big, big to do when they had them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where would they set up the tents?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, right out in the woods.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Right in, right on Cedar Creek?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, not, somewhere around there. They usually had it between Cedar Creek and Southwark, is where they used to have it all the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So people would come from both places?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: All places.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would there be usually the same denomination that would put these on?

speaker: Frances Fry
words: Well, I don't think so. I don't remember. They just had the meetings and then everybody that wanted to, to... Because afterwards, I know they'd, but whether they...
